en: Dīpaṃkarabhadra’s *Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi*. Homage to Vajrasattva!

Having bowed to the true secret wheel of Mañjuśrī, which is liberated from the obscurations of the knowable and so forth, and endowed with the mirror of primordial wisdom and other qualities, I shall speak of it for my own recollection, according to the system of the glorious *Samāja* and following the sequence of the oral tradition of the wheels. 1. From here on, [I shall proceed] according to the method of the glorious *Samāja*.
He who has been consecrated by the guru with the water and other [empowerments] permitted thereafter,
through the secret and wisdom empowerments in this secret wheel for the attainment of reality,
becomes a knower of the secret, a knower of the reality of yoga, and a knower of the reality of the union of the three vehicles.

One who understands, according to the principles of the tantra, the classification of the vidyās, heart-mantras, and mudrās, as well as the three types of samādhi and both common and extraordinary accomplishments;
or one who abides in the commitments and vows and is intensely devoted to the yoga of wisdom (prajñā).
One who knows the application of mantra and tantra is fit for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

However, even if one possesses yoga, fortitude, and so forth, if they are not endowed with the aforementioned qualities, they are not at all fit for the welfare of sentient beings; for these qualities are what constitute such a person as "good."
Compassionate, firm in his vows, a practitioner of recitation, faithful, and a knower of the profound reality, he—
remaining established in his own wheel after performing the preliminary service— should draw the mandala in some place agreeable to the mind, smeared with genuine sandalwood and other substances. (7)
Having first arranged [the offerings] in the morning upon a surface strewn with fragrant flowers,

and having meditated on the syllable *maṃ*, blazing like the Lord, within the moon-disk at the heart for the sake of purifying the gates of liberation and for the increase of merit, one should perform the recitation and other rites.
Standing before the Buddhas arisen in all directions and throughout the three times,
one performs worship according to the ritual procedure by means of forms and other qualities arising from the light of the heart.
One then [confesses] the evil deeds committed throughout the three times, which arise solely from one's own false conceptualizations.
I confess all [misdeeds] three times, like a dream within a dream.

Having rejoiced without exception in whatever is auspicious and virtuous belonging to the Perfectly Awakened Ones, their true sons, the Noble Ones, and others, I subsequently dedicate it toward complete awakening.
I pray that she who grants the consolation of all hopes for all Buddhas,
who abides in the space of their teaching, may shine forth, faultless, throughout the entire world—
I go for refuge to the perfectly awakened Buddhas, who bestow the fruits of the welfare of both self and others;
I fully approach for refuge the true Dharma of all excellent beings, which consists of scripture and realization, and which is the inconceivable basis of all true excellence.
I have gone for refuge to the assembly that has attained confidence, which is irreversible, endowed with the fruits such as the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), born of the secret initiation,
the excellent path of the Son of the Lord of Sages, and characterized by conduct leading to infinite and supreme awakening. (16)
Therefore, now I take refuge through the true awakening that is the self-nature of all Buddhas.
For the sake of awakening from deluded views, I direct my entire mind toward enlightenment—the abode of the nectar of infinite wisdom that eradicates all obscurations. (17–18)
Buddhahood arises from the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), for the cause and its fruit are non-attached;
because my nature is a reality to be personally realized, I am indeed of the essence of the wisdom of emptiness.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
And also the syllable HŪṂ, as well as the Uṣṇīṣas such as Śāśvata and the rest.
For the sake of protection, one situated within the wheel of wrath should meditate while crushing the obstructors. Then, one should meditate on the Dharmadhātu as a white triangle standing upright,
possessing variegated light that revolves through the directions, and containing within it a lotus and vajra situated below the void.
Therein, arising from the wheel of the syllable *bhrūṃ*, is the manifestation of the eternal one together with the Vidyā;
it pervades the sky with an expanding flood of Buddhas, is endowed with the square [mandala] and other features,
is presided over by the moon and sun, and has the seat of the deity upon a universal lotus.
One should visualize a gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) in which all excellent jewels are distributed;
it is endowed with the characteristics of vowels and possesses rays of light from the consonants beginning with *ka*.
Having visualized that moon of gnosis (*jñānacandra*) as the mind upon a moon-seat in the center, [one should proceed]. 23–24.
There, one should visualize a red vajra arising from the first heart-mantra, joined with that same first heart-mantra;
having assumed the pride of being that very [deity],
one whose body has the nature of a Jina, with limbs and face like crystal, blue on the right side and red on the other.
Exalted by the excellence of all supreme aspects, with the sky as his garment adorned with the ornaments of true virtues;
embraced by the noble Prajñā with two arms, he is firmly seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture;
holding a vajra and a sword in his right hands, and a fine jewel and a lotus in his left.
One should meditate upon oneself as Samantabhadra, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, the glorious refuge of the world’s prosperity, radiating light in all directions.
Having observed that world— the vessel— to be disciplined through great passion...
One should cause the assembly of Jinas to enter within one's own heart by means of the sound of the mantra.

Then, having projected the goddesses of the true vidyās— such as Locanā and the others— who consist of the objects of the senses such as form, in nine ways, one should cause them to enter into the interior of one's own vidyā.
Having fashioned within his own wife, who is like a *karkaṭī* melon, a maṇḍala arisen from sexual union,
he should cause the entire world to enter therein for its consolation;
[he does so] with the excellent Buddhas pervading the sky, who arise from the fluid produced within his own vajra.
One should serve [the teacher] for the sake of non-retrogression and to attain the fruit of the knowledge of reality.
Having seen that world comforted by seeds born of its own nature, one should then release all sentient beings, who are born from the nature of the mind of the world.
One should [visualize] the six [bodhisattvas] beginning with Kṣitigarbha, whose natures are the eye and so forth,
from the seed-syllables *kṣiṃ*, *jraṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *skaṃ*, and *saṃ* respectively;
and the six [consorts] beginning with Rūpavajrā, who arise from the nature of the external and internal [objects].

With *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*, and *khaṃ*, as well as from the seed-syllable *raṃ*, one should [invite] those vidyās beginning with Locanā who abide outside; and with *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, and *tāṃ*, those born from the reality of the world, phenomena, the self, and the [ultimate] principle, who arise from the nature of earth and the other elements. (35–36)
One should emit the Perfectly Awakened Ones, beginning with Śāśvata, who are born from the intrinsic nature of the aggregates such as form,
by means of *buṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, and *bhiḥ*, and all phenomena by means of *khaṃ* and *hūṃ*.
Then, that mind— marked with *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ*— is interlaced between the two radiant arms.
For the sake of purifying the gentle outflow, one should meditate on [the deity] residing within the interior of the secret lotus;
and those [deities], ignited by the fire of passion and having liquefied the two bodies, should be well-impelled by the songs of the goddesses of the directions who shine like true friends. (38–39)
O Vajra-Mind, Lord of the World, protect me, O realm of beings, with your delightful pleasures for those who desire the great purpose!
Embrace me, O Father, all-pervading supreme kinsman, if you wish for my life to continue, O Protector!
You are the Vajra-Body, the wheel of commands beloved by many beings, who perceives the welfare of the ultimate goal of awakening and the purpose of the Buddhas.
"O Lord, if you wish for me to live, desire me who am in union with passion through passion!

(41) O Vajravāca, you who are compassionate toward the welfare of all and always engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world—O Samantabhadra, if you wish for me to live, O Lord, enjoy me in the practice of delightful love! (42)

O Vajrakāma, supreme of commitments, you who act for the great benefit of others, the ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and compassionate through equanimity— desire me, the treasury of virtues, who am like a multitude of jewels, if you, O Lord, desire my life!
(43) Seeing that [the world] was as if in calamity due to the lack of one who would rouse it from its lethargy, he acted with haste.
Having contemplated the reality as being like an illusion, the meaning of one's own mantra should arise once more.
[The deity] has a face with a base of saffron color, blue on the right and white on the other;
he has the appearance of a youth’s ornaments and is uniquely beautiful through the bliss of wisdom.
Embraced by the true Prajñā with two arms, he holds in his mouths the Prajñā who is of his own nature;
his hands bear a radiant sword, an excellent arrow, a blue lotus, and a bow;
he has brought the three worlds to completion through the emanations of the multitude of manifest Buddhas.
Mañjuvajra himself arises from the sign produced by his own seed-syllable.
Through attachment to existence, existence becomes infinite; through attachment to peace, one partakes in misfortune.
By cultivating intimacy with illusion, one becomes identical with the Dharmadhātu.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the dharmadhātu.
Having produced its outflow through virtuous friends, it reaches omniscience through maturation;
that which is the locus of the eye and so forth is held to be the *upasādhana*.
[It is characterized] by the Lord of the Earth, Vajra, Ākāśa, Lokeśa, Skambha, and Bhadraka.
Having filled the eyes and other sense organs with their respective seed-syllables, one should carry forth the human [body].
The fulfillment of the world's welfare consists in carrying forth the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa [bodies];
therefore, for the sake of accomplishment, there should be the consecration of the secrets of the mind and so forth.

Having meditated upon the secret deities of mind and so forth— Vajra, Padma, and Cakra— residing within the moon disks at one's own heart, throat, and head as the true lords born from *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ*,
[one should contemplate them] with rays of light such as Vajra-rūpa, which arise from the contact of their hearts with the limbs of the Prajñā.

Having fully worshipped all the Vināyakas who pervade all directions and the three times, one should then request the presence of Cittavajra and the others— who reside in the heart, throat, and head of those [Vināyakas] who possess the wealth of their fulfilled purpose— at their respective seats of empowerment.
May the glorious Holder of the Mind-Vajra, who is meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment of the Mind-Vajra.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras, [grant this].
May those who possess the vajra-mind grant me the state of empowerment today.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the mind-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
The glorious Dharma, the path of speech, is cultivated as the indivisibility of the three vajras;
may it today grant me the state of empowerment for the Vajra of Speech.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, cultivated as the indivisibility of the three vajras, [grant this].
May those who hold the vajra of speech grant me the state of empowerment today!
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
May the glorious Holder of the Body-Vajra, who is cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment as a Body-Vajra-holder.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras, [grant this].
May the Body-Vajra holders grant me the state of empowerment today.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the body-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
He stated that they perform the purification of the sixteen recollections;
however, the empowerment of his mind and so forth was not mentioned, as it would have been an irrelevant statement.
Having observed the characteristics of the three secrets, [one proceeds] through union with the limbs of the illusory wisdom (*māyā-prajñā*).
For the sake of softening, purifying, and cleansing [the disciple], the "Great Accomplishment" (mahāsādhana) is prescribed:

having exhorted the Protectors residing in the various directions with the light from the heart of the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva), one should [sprinkle] the disciple with the waters of nectar from filled jars produced by the vidyās arising from that light. // 62–63 //
The glorious Lord, duly consecrated and possessing the supreme crown of the Lord of the Family (kuleśa),
should purify his own consort, Prajñā, by means of the [five] outflows and so forth, as well as the central [mantras].
He should [place] the individual atoms [of the mantras] at her head, heart, navel, secret place, and the ends of her feet.

Having filled [the heart] with the syllables *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, *svā*, and *hṛt*, and with *āḥ* and *hā*, which consist of the families beginning with Śāśvata; having purified the eight-petaled lotus at the heart with the five Perfect Buddhas (*pañcasambuddha*)—namely *hūṃ* and *āḥ*—one who possesses the excellent vajra (*sadvajra*) should cause the Buddhas to be impassioned (*anurāgayet*) by means of that [lotus]. //32, 65–66//
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that impassions all Tathāgatas.
Having established within oneself the maṇḍala of Buddhas pervading the sky through the radiance of the heart-moon and sword, which is the nature of the true mind situated upon a vajra-lotus,
one generates one’s own wheel there by means of its seed-syllable and makes it firm.
One should emit [the deities] according to this rite for the purification of ignorance within the worlds.
Having exhorted the Lord Akṣobhya, the Victor who accomplishes the purpose of great aversion,
one should emit him with the mantra "Vajradhṛk," possessing the luster of a sapphire.
White on the left and red on the other side, endowed with the arms of Paramādya, the illustrious one,
having withdrawn [the deity] into himself, should establish him through all states of being.
And [he should worship] the Lord who acts for the sake of great delusion, whose first appearance is "Jinajig."
Likewise, one should meditate upon [the Lord] on the eastern lunar disc as being endowed with the wheel of truth and so forth;

and on the south, one should meditate upon the Lord Ratneśa, known as "Holder of Jewels" (Ratnadhṛk), who is golden-hued, full of vigor, possesses a youthful face, and is endowed with excellent jewels and other attributes. (71–72)

"ĀROLI" refers to Vāgīśa, the Lord who effects the purpose of great passion; he has the luster of a ruby and holds a lotus, with a youthful face at his back. "Prajñādhṛk" refers to Amogheśa, born from the sky, who effects the purpose of great envy.
One should meditate on the one with the face of a youth, possessing the luster of beryl, holding a sword and other implements in the north (74).

All [the deities] should be visualized upon a lotus and sun mandala, wearing matted hair and crowns, united with their respective female consorts, and adorned with all ornaments and fine garments (75).
In the southeast, Moharati (Delusion-Delight) bestows the purpose of compassion and skillful means;
she is Locanā, whose nature is like that of the Lord of the Body, situated within her own lunar mandala.
In the southwest, Dveṣarati (Hatred-Delight) bestows loving-kindness, aspiration, and the fulfillment of desires.
Māmakī, eager for the vow like Citteśa, is in the moon-maṇḍala;
she who bestows joy, strength, and samādhi as "Rāgarati" is in the northwest.
Pāṇḍarā, pure through the purpose of Vāgīśā’s burden, is in the moon-maṇḍala. (77–78)
And this other one is called Vajrarati; she is the accomplisher of the knowledge of equanimity.
She has the same nature as Ratneśa, and Tārā is beautiful upon the moon.
[Her symbols are] a wheel, a divine red lotus, a yellow lotus, and a blue lotus.
The remaining [deities] are taught to have the same signs as their own lords; therefore, their sequence is as follows:

in the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), and on both sides of the eastern gate, are Rūpā and the others with mirrors and so forth, and Kāyā and the others appearing through the three principles (tattva). (80–81)
At the eastern gate is Yamāntaka, who is radiant with the form of Citteśa and seated in the wrathful posture;
he is the destroyer of diseases because he annihilates the aggregates and the objects of knowledge. At the western gate is Aparājita, who is terrifying with fierce eyes like those of Kāyeśa.

"Prājñāntakṛt" (the end-maker of the state of consciousness) is the destroyer of desire, because of the abandonment of the afflictions through the vision of one's own self. He is the destroyer of the evil of death and birth; at the rear door, he is Aśvakandhara.
"Padmāntakṛt" (the end-maker of the lotus) is the destroyer of desire, agitated by the fierce Vāgīśā.
Akṣobhya, the destroyer of fierce obstacles, is in the north, as is Amṛtakuṇḍalin;
Vighnāntakṛt is [in the east] through the purification of the door-activities and the enemies of the gods.
Their eyebrows are knitted, their hair blazes upward, and they have brown hair, eyebrows, beards, and eyes.
With their mouths agape and tongues lolling, they laugh fiercely with bared fangs;
these [deities] have hands holding fierce mallets, staffs, lotuses, vajras, and so forth,
their bodies adorned with cruel serpents, and they embrace their respective consorts.
Having visualized the completed wheel in its own nature on all sides,
and having seen the Buddhas drawn into the form of the wheel by the goads of the seed-syllables at the heart,
one should dispel the obstacles with those [deities] who destroy their own obstacles and protect [the site].
Having offered the *argha* water consecrated with mantra and mixed with flowers such as the *candra*,
one should place that wheel into the [central] wheel; then, having empowered it with the eyes, body, and so forth,
one should meditate upon it as being sprinkled as before, ranging from the outflow (*niṣyanda*) up to the highest degree.
Akṣobhya is on the crowns of the Buddhas; the remaining [Buddhas] are sprinkled by their own lords.
The gatekeepers are considered to be [consecrated] by Kāyeśa, Akṣobhya, Vāgīśa, and Citteśa.
Having thus sprinkled [them], [the practitioner] [visualizes the deity] placed within the lotus of wisdom by means of the radiance from his own heart.

Having worshipped oneself and the Lords of Sages with the rays of Rūpavajrā and the others, which emerge from the pores of the skin starting from form (rūpa), are released from the lord of the peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra), and spread to the ends of space— one becomes the essence of both the worshipper and the object of worship. // 92–93 //
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas.
One should praise the wheel with all dharmas, which are the embodiments of the Perfectly Awakened One’s own self;
[one should praise] the five wisdoms through the mudrās, the five hundred families, and the triad:
"Akṣobhyavajra, Great Wisdom, Vajradhātu, Great Sage! (94)
O you who are the three mandalas, the supreme of the three vajras, the Vajra of Sound—homage be to you!
(95) O Vairocana, great purity, Vajra-peace, great delight, supreme pinnacle of natural luminosity—O Vajra of the Directions, homage be to you! (96)
O King of Jewels, most profound, stainless as the space of the vajra-sky;
pure by nature, unstained—homage be to you, Vajra Body!
97 O Vajra Amita, Great King, free from conceptual construction, bearer of the vajra of space!
Homage be to you, Vajra of Speech, who has attained the perfection of passion!
98 O Amoghavajra, perfectly awakened one, fulfiller of all hopes, born of the nature of purity—homage be to you, Vajrasattva! 99

Having meditated upon [the vessel] containing the fragrance of water-medicines from the moon and sun, situated within the wheels of wind and fire, presided over by the *praṇava*, possessing radiance, consecrated with the three principles (*tritattva*), and filled with the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), one whose tongue is joined with the vajra by the syllable *hūṃ*— 100. Having meditated upon [the vessel] containing the fragrance of water-medicines from the moon and sun, situated within the wheels of wind and fire, presided over by the *praṇava*, possessing radiance, consecrated with the three principles (*tritattva*), and filled with the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), one whose tongue is joined with the vajra by the syllable *hūṃ*—
One should satisfy the entire mandala situated within the moon at the heart by means of that [nectar].

Having made the world consist of the nature of the Buddhas through the Lords created from the rays of light from the heart—[Lords] who are free from one's own false conceptualizations—one should cause them to enter into the interior of the seed-syllable at the heart. (101–102)
Having meditated on one's own mind as radiant, situated within the central seed-syllable at the heart-center in the form of the moon and the bindu, one should cause the Jñānasattva to shine forth;
and having awakened the Vajras of Mind, Speech, and Body by means of a garland of light rays.
One should meditate upon that [wisdom] which is established in the heart, flowing with the nectar of one's own knowledge.
Then, having illuminated the entire body from within on all sides by means of that [wisdom], one fulfills the welfare of the world through the arrays of light radiating from every pore. 104–105.
Having meditated upon one's own subtle emblem, or the circle of sages (municakra) situated at the tip of the nose of the Vidyā— self-realized and radiant through union with true wisdom—
one should perceive the sign of stability by means of the signs of its radiating rays.
One should repeatedly perform [the rite] with the various signs of the Buddhas.
From the true vajra of body, speech, and mind, one should recite the mantra while emanating rays of light from the five true gnoses, either simultaneously or sequentially. (107–108)

One should recite while causing the wheel of the nature of reality (dharmatā) of the vajra-lotus—which resides in the vajras of body, speech, and mind—to become firm as a dwelling place and radiating the gnosis-body (jñānakāya).
One should utter the mantra, which is withdrawn by the measure of the breaths, while radiating it with the vital energies (prāṇas). 109.
One should perform the recitation through the expansion and withdrawal of the body and so forth, both sequentially and non-sequentially.

Having thus uttered [the mantra], one pervades space with those rays of light from the body and so forth; as before, emitting a flood of vidyās from the vital breath, which is worthy of worship by the true mind. (110–111)

One should finally dissolve into one's own self the stream of Buddhas of the *āyāma* lineage, who have been brought under control by the force of immersion in the bliss of the shimmering, perfectly hidden Vidyā. Furthermore,
[one should do so] through the resolute convictions (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the *niṣyanda* and other [emanations], arising from the drop (*bindu*), the subtle [point], and the three secrets.
The meditations are likewise [classified] by the divisions of "mild" and so forth, just like the practices of service and the rest.

(113) Through the contemplation of the reality within one's own heart, and by the movement of the limited mind, one should worship the mandala after having entreated it with the songs sung by the assembly of Locanā and the other goddesses. (114)

One should cause [the nectar] to fall according to the ritual rule from the moon at the crown of the head— which is moistened by the *praṇava*— down through the channel of the mind's water, thereby bringing satisfaction to the body, speech, and mind.
Having thus performed the recitation while resting, the wise practitioner, having completed the worship and other rites, [should proceed].
One should dismiss the Buddhas who have been invoked as the essence of the three principles, free from attachment.
(54) Having thus beheld the entire world as liberated through the vision of reality, one should, out of compassion, bring forth the aspiration for their welfare. (116–117)
Having arisen from meditative absorption and maintaining pride in his Lord,
he, while engaged in the practice of movement, should fully worship the objects of the Perfectly Awakened One’s domain—
those which follow the nature of the objects of the glorious Mañjuvajra, who is the self of all. 118.
Meditating thus upon the sense objects as established through their respective purities—
those [objects] whose nature is eternal and so forth, which abide as the dharmas within each individual,
and which possess the form of the glorious Vajradhara— one is endowed with a pure being. (119–120)
Free from improper intentions, one should accomplish every task;
this worship of the infinite wheel of reality is always immeasurable for the excellent yogin.
[One should offer] the Lord of one's own wheel within the moon of one's heart, along with one's own food, by means of one's own seed-syllables.
Having fully grasped [the nectar] through the principles of one's own heart, which has been rendered the immortality of all Buddhas;
pure by virtue of being the nature of all phenomena and consecrated by the three principles—one should worship it, thereby pleasing the true wheel of one’s own presiding deity. (122–123)
This external person is an object of inference; however, the mental one arises from mind alone.

But this unsurpassed [state] results from the burning away of the fuel of the aggregate of the fire of knowledge by means of all these very desires, which are born from one's own destiny, self, and inherent nature. (124)
One should likewise honor others; this is the commitment (samaya) held by the Sugatas.

Whatever actions of body and so forth one performs while honoring all the Buddhas, one should always perform them with a concentrated mind in a manner appropriate for the welfare of the world. 125–126.
Whatever great action consisting of body and speech, which is of the nature of mudrās and mantras,
having performed each such action, one should worship all the Buddhas.
Even when the object is one and the same, mental constructions appear in various forms.
Since the arising of liberation, suffering, and pleasure all result from the remainder of karma,
therefore auspicious and inauspicious karma— consisting of body and so forth— is born of conceptual construction.
How could there be such construction in a gnosis that is free from all conceptual constructions?
Amoghavajrasaccakrī, for the sake of awakening the samaya,
should meditate on the *kha* of the heart-action-vajra and consecrate [the disciple] with universal purity.
In cases of faults such as disrespect toward the guru, one should always bring about the consumption of food.
Abiding within one's own wheel, one should perform the external bath according to the ritual of consecration (sekavidhāna).
Even during the intervals between the junctions of the day (sandhyā), having performed worship and recitation as before,
one should sleep endowed with wisdom and compassion, with the true wheel situated within the heart.
At the time of rising, the illustrious beginner, urged by the song of the goddess,
should rise in the morning and recite [the mantra] as before;
he should be endowed with the vows of mantra and moral conduct, and have his eyes, body, and so forth, consecrated.
Having attained some degree of immersion in gnosis, one should recite [mantras] during the twilights without weariness.
Having mastered the power of gnosis, one who has fully perfected all aspects and performs the emanation and reabsorption [of the universe] should constantly rely upon yoga to some extent. (134–135)

Mastering right knowledge and meditating, the yogi should perform deeds for the welfare of the world by means of the atoms of the elements, which consist of the triple reality (*trisacca*) and have the nature of reflected images. Having repeatedly attained the signs of perfection, he indeed acts thus.
Having performed the worship of the three principles according to the rule, one should draw the mandala.
Standing within the wheel and having recited the mantra according to the rule— whether requested by oneself or for the sake of others—
even while striving for the benefit of others, one should draw it upon perceiving the auspicious sign.
One should recite the mantra of the Discus-bearer (Cakrin) one hundred thousand times, or one hundred thousand times for one's own tutelary deity;
for others who possess the Discus, one should properly write [the mantras] ten thousand times by command.
One should perform the emissions containing the three principles (*tritattva*) and others containing the seed-syllable of the heart (*hṛdbīja*).
One should extract the mantras from the names, beginning with the syllables accompanied by the anusvāra.

That which is known as the secret of body, speech, and mind—possessing the nature of action, phenomena, and the great self—is the pledge (samaya) of the three secrets; it is called the mudrā, the seed-syllable, and the heart-mantra.
But the Vidyā is said to be the agent of action because it impels pacification and the other rites;

the Mālā-mantras are also called Vidyās, so the wise man should recite them in every way. Having performed the recitation according to the proper application and having obtained permission from his own lord and others, [he should proceed].
Having folded one’s legs in the posture of cessation, one should draw [the mandala] from the purity of one’s own mind.

Having expelled the obstructors, sprinkled the ground with water after sweeping it, and having made supplications and requests, one should perform the three samādhis and cause the Buddhas and others to dwell [in the site]. (143–144)
Having offered the bali and argha, worshipped [the deity], and nourished [the site] with fire-oblations (homa), one should place it in the sky.
One should dig the earth so that it is free from obstacles; this same procedure applies even when filling a pit.
[The practitioner], having previously cultivated the habitual practice and possessing the self-yoga of Mañjuvajra, [should proceed].
Having consecrated the site of the mandala and being endowed with worship through the [deities] to be withdrawn,
one who abides in the yoga of the wheel of the enemy of obstacles should receive self-consecration;
thus, one should indeed cut down the wicked through yoga or through one's own presiding deity.
With the mantra *oṃ bhūḥ kham*, one should transform the earth, which has become like space,
into the nature of a vajra with *hūṃ laṃ hūṃ*, and then consecrate it:
*oṃ medini vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ*.
As before, he is the self of the yoga that destroys obstacles, possessing devotion at the beginning and end of service;
he is the primordial yogin who emits his own wheel and is the nectar at its conclusion. He is the self of the supreme yoga of the King of Wheels, performing the excellent rites of the wheels.
The *Karmarājāgriyoga* is the supreme triad of meditative absorptions (samādhi).
The master established in this yoga possesses the form of the essence of all Buddhas;
with the nature of the pure vajra, he abides in the center of the mandala circle. // 150–151 //
The Hero, holding the vajra and bell, should be requested [to act] in the manifestation of the three wheels,
together with his companions who hold the vajra and bell and whose forms consist of the nature of Śāśvata and the others.
[He is] the peaceful one of all Tathāgatas, the abode of all Tathāgatas.
Teach the supreme maṇḍala, the foremost selflessness of all phenomena;
the supreme maṇḍala, complete with all characteristics yet devoid of all characteristics, the pinnacle of Samantabhadra’s body. 153–154.
Arising from the supreme, peaceful dharmas, purifying the conduct of gnosis,
and the foremost speech of Samantabhadra— speak of the supreme mandala!
It is the great mind of all sentient beings, pure and naturally stainless.
O Samantabhadra, supreme mind, O voice, charioteer of the maṇḍala!
Having observed that realm of sentient beings thus enveloped in darkness, Mañjurāj became enraged;
uttering "HŪṂ VAJRA UTTIṢṬHA," he raised his own eye, the emanated wheel. (156–157)
With eyes like the moon and sun emitting sparks, illuminating all directions throughout the three times,
the wise one, surveying the world, should circumambulate the mandala ground;
with a thunderbolt blazing from the soles of his feet, he should be intent on brandishing that vajra.
Dancing with the playful vajra-step and uttering the fierce *hūṃ* with bared fangs, he shall drive away the hosts of the wicked, the circles of obstacles such as the gods and others.
Let all the multitudes of obstacles residing in body, speech, and mind listen! (159–160)
I am the glorious Mañjurava, the employer of the protection wheel;
with a vajra of blazing form, I shatter those born of the three bodies. Should anyone transgress against me, they shall be shattered here—there is no other way. 161, 93.
Having taken possession of the ground, one should drive in stakes to ensure there are no obstacles:
OṂ GHA GHA GHĀTAYA 2 SARVADUṢṬĀN PHAṬ KĪLAYA 2 SARVAPĀPĀN PHAṬ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ VAJRAKĪLA VAJRADHARA ĀJÑĀPAYATI SARVADUṢṬAKĀYAVĀKCITTAVAJRAṂ KĪLAYA HŪṂ PHAṬ //
One should mentally drive a stake into the center [of the ground], which has its roots below and its obstacles and enemies above;
thus one shall destroy all the multitudes of obstacles situated throughout the ten directions.
Having surveyed the earth as being free from obstacles and possessing a radiance filled with sharp flames—
Having mentally established the boundaries, the enclosure walls, and the directional bindings, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana):
"O Goddess, you are the witness of all the Tathāgatas, the Protectors, regarding the specificities of the conduct and methods, and the perfections of the stages. (164–165)
Just as the army of Māra was shattered by the Protector Śākyasiṃha,
so too, having conquered the army of Māra, I shall draw the maṇḍala.
Having smeared the ground with fragrant substances and the like, and having scattered various flowers upon it...
The wise one should construct the mandala in the place of the wheel-bearers, beginning with Candra and the others (167).
Having invoked the true wheel there and performed the binding of the boundaries and so forth,
he should perform the worship, praise, and tasting of nectar, and consecrate the vases (168).
One should consecrate the pitchers of the maṇḍala deities with their respective mantras— pitchers whose fine necks are covered with cloth and which are provided with sprouts of mango and other trees—
along with a collection of the wheel [of deities] consisting of the five grains, medicinal herbs, jewels, fragrant water, and the [mandala] circle.
One should perform the recitation with the Lord of the Wheel at the head, his crown bound with a garland of vajras.
Having offered the *argha* and performed worship, one should cast white flowers and a vessel of lotus containing excellent perfumes and the like, which has been scented with incense. (170–171)
Having offered the bali offering daily at the three junctions of the day, one should likewise recite the mantra.
They [the deities] are in the outer corners of the wheel, and Jaya is to the right of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa).
Having poured water from that [water] into the argha vessel, by means of that, one performs the consecration.
There shall be the water-consecration for oneself and all the disciples.
Having performed the worship of the wheel again and raising incense with the hand, the wise one, kneeling on the ground, should pray to the Lord of the Wheel and to the Buddhas.

O Blessed One, Mañjuśrīvajra, King of Vidyās, homage be to you! O Protector whose nature is compassion, I desire to draw the maṇḍala out of compassion for the disciples and for the sake of worshipping you. (175)
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to grant your grace to me, your devotee. May the Buddhas— who bestow the purpose of the wheel of activity for the world— take heed of me,
as well as the Bodhisattvas established in the fruit and whatever other mantra-deities there may be.
The deities, the world-protectors, and the spirits who have been instructed in perfect enlightenment, those beings who delight in the teaching, and whoever possesses the vajra-eye—
[I,] such-and-such a one, the great Vajrin, [enter] the Mañjuśrī-arising maṇḍala.
I shall write this for the purification of the world, according to my capacity and with due ritual offerings.
Out of compassion, may you all, together with your disciples, deign to be present within the mandala. (179–180)
Having thus invited them three times and performed the worship and other rites for the Lord,
he went outside with his disciples—
who were wise, highly energetic, grateful, and free from egoism— holding garlands and water-pots.
One should accommodate those of noble birth, virtuous, faithful, endowed with beauty, complexion, and youth, as well as those who are seekers and diligent in the accomplishment of mantras;
one may even accept those who are deformed, devoid of virtues, or lowly. (182–183)
The ritual procedure for the mandala is authorized for all four assemblies—
those who are disciplined in their respective trainings and whose minds delight in the Mahāyāna.
Some who seek the accomplishment of mantras enter here into the mandala.
Others besides those desire merit, while others seek the sake of the next world.
Having set the next world as his goal and having cultivated great faith, the wise man should enter the maṇḍala; he should not strive for a fruit of this world.
"For one who desires results in this world, the results in the next world are not so great;
but for a man seeking the sake of the next world, the results in this world are indeed abundant.
Having spoken thus to those disciples, he placed them within his own mind through his intellect.
As before, one should request those who are purified by the vajra-lotus at this gate:
"You are my teacher, O Great Passion;
O Great Lord, I desire the firm method of great awakening. (188–189)
Grant me the commitment, grant me the reality and the bodhicitta;
grant me the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the Three Refuges. O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation. 190

Having recited those [mantras] three times and having ascertained that the disciples are devoted and affectionate toward the True Dharma, he should appoint one principal disciple and speak these words:
"Come, child! This is the method of the Mahāyāna, the system of mantra practice."
I shall teach you correctly, for you are a worthy vessel for the Great Way.
The Buddhas arisen throughout the three times, who possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras.
By means of this incomparable application of mantra, the exceedingly terrible and mighty army of Māra was shattered by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas;
having conformed to the ways of the world and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, they have attained parinirvāṇa. (194)

Therefore, my child, apply this mind toward the attainment of omniscience. (195) The teacher should first cause the threefold proclamation of the teaching and so forth; then, he should generate the bodhicitta that has not yet arisen, or cause it to be remembered again if it has already arisen. (196)
Having performed all the rites and protected [the disciple], one should meditate upon the heart, throat, and head;
one should place the vajra, lotus, and wheel, along with the syllables *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ*, respectively.
Reciting "Hūṃ Oṃ Āḥ" in this manner, one should apply [the substances] with the fist of the fragrance-water-vajra.
Having touched the heart, head, and throat, one should offer flowers and so forth in sequence.
One should place the flower on the head, incense before [the deity], and the lamp and perfume again at the heart.
Having performed all these and recited the mantra, the ascetic should respectfully bestow them upon the disciples.

One should provide a tooth-stick made from the tips of *aśvattha* or *udumbara* branches that are twelve finger-breadths long, free of insects, unsplit, and without blemishes; it should not be crooked.
Having used these while facing either east or north, one should then discard them.
On ground smeared with an area the size of a cow’s hide, one should bestow accomplishments such as pacification and the like.
Having sipped water and offered three mouthfuls [of water], and having settled [the disciple] outside,
one should well protect the *kuśa* grass intended for the bed and pillow with arm-threads.
The mantra for drinking three sips of water.
Oṃ hrīḥ! O Pure Dharma, purify all the misdeeds of this person and remove all conceptual constructions! Hūṃ!
When does the appearance of the Omniscient Ones occur in the world, or does it not?
Like the flower of the udumbara tree, it may happen only once in a great while. Even more difficult than that to arise is the practice of the way of mantra.
By means of which they, remaining unextinguished, are indeed able to accomplish incomparable benefit for sentient beings.
Whatever evil was previously committed over many millions of eons,
all of that goes to destruction upon seeing such a mandala.
How much more so for one who abides in the system of mantra practice and recites the mantras of the Protectors; such a person indeed attains the unsurpassed state.
For them, rebirth in the miserable realms—the source of all suffering—is utterly severed. (206)
For those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this supreme practice—
today you, O great-souled ones, have obtained incomparable gains,
since you have been accepted here into the teaching by all the Victors together with their Sons.
"Being born, you have all been taken into the care of the Great Beings;
therefore, tomorrow you shall indeed be born into the Mahāyāna.
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna. (209)
"By means of this, you shall become Tathāgatas when you depart.
Having performed the teaching and the protection, you should sleep upon a bed of kuśa grass. Whatever you see in your dreams, you shall tell me in the morning. (210–211)
Having performed the protection, empowerment, and other preliminary rites, one should recite that mantra which accomplishes all activities (*sārvakarmika*).

Kuṇḍalī, belonging to the five families and the three wheels, is the performer of all activities. Having inquired about an auspicious or inauspicious dream, one should destroy any inauspiciousness with Kuṇḍalī.

Having protected those worthy disciples, he should then cause them to take the vow. O Lord, having bestowed the irreversible consecration in the mandala, please tell me the reality of the mandala and the deity, as well as the preparatory rites for the preceptor.
"I shall always be the preceptor for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings— the commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow.
Having caused the disciples who seek the state of a preceptor to take up this vow, [he should proceed].
Having established yoga and fully worshipped the true wheel, one should mentally place it in the sky—
appearing in the form of Śāśvata and the others, arising from the seed-syllables of their respective colors,
endowed with the five gnoses, and divided into twenty-five parts. // 216–217 //
He whose eyes are the sun and moon arising from the syllable *yaḥ*, whose body is the very form of Mañjuvajra—
having drawn [the object] with a blazing gaze like a hook, he places it within his own color,
together with Vairocana and the others, along with the Wisdom-thread of the Heart that accomplishes all.
Bestow the eternal thread for the purpose of weaving your own wheel,
containing the three principles (tritattva) as its core, while seeking the state of Akṣobhya and recollecting that "all phenomena are mutually interpenetrating," and so forth. 219–220.
Twice as long as the wheel and one-twentieth the width of the door,
it should be moistened with the five nectars and fragrant substances and protected;
then the yogi, holding the thread, should move it while contained within the three syllables.
Having summoned him with three *jjaḥ* sounds— and likewise saying "jjaḥ, jjaḥ, jjaḥ" himself once more— the illustrious one,
standing facing westward in the southern direction, should grasp his left fist at the navel and cast the celestial thread;
in the same manner, he should extend the lower thread.
Oṃ, do not transgress the vajra-samaya-line! Hūṃ!
The time has come for you to act for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, with the sound of the sutra, you should urge the Tathāgatas who pervade the sky to come here.
[Those who dwell] in the directions of the lords of yakṣas, pretas, and nāgas, and those who reside in fire and wind—[you should urge them as well].
Having first laid out the threads for the four directions— east, west, north, and south— and outside them,
having likewise laid out the diagonal threads starting from the southeast and southwest,
one should likewise [draw] the eightfold maṇḍala for the directions east, west, north, and south.
Having doubled that thread and fixed it in the center of the circle,
one should then [draw] two vajra-threads outside the circular shape; furthermore,
in the northeast, one should draw the Cakravāḍa mountain, proceeding clockwise in due order.
The wise one, maintaining equanimity toward all directions, should lay out the lines with the cord.
If there are no signs, there will be failure; if the cord is broken, the preceptor suffers loss.
From a deficiency or excess [in measurement], diseases arise; from confusion regarding the directions, the disciple falls into error.
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
provided with four lines, and decorated with silk bands, garlands, and festoons;
[it is likewise adorned] in all the corner sections and at the junctions of the gate-turrets.
One should trace the outer maṇḍala, inlaid with vajra-jewels;
inside that, a wheel resembling eight maṇḍalas,
circular on all sides and half the size of the outer wheel.

One should divide the auspicious [mandala], which is constructed with wheel-pillars and the like and surrounded by a garland of vajras; then, one should open the door with the syllable *hrīḥ* and the wrathful gaze. The door is considered to be one-eighth of the circle and is thought to be without a pedestal (*vedikā*).
The *niryūhas* and the deity-bands (*devatāpaṭṭikā*) are equal in measure to the doors.
On all sides, the altar (*vedī*), the cheek (*kapola*), and the wing (*pakṣaka*) are half the size of the door.
There are bands for the *hara*, the *ardhahāra*, the moon, and the sun, as well as bands for garlands and strings of pearls.

The ground for the colored powder (rajobhūmi) is half the size of that; outside the ground for the root-line (mūlasūtra), the ground for the lines of the pillars and so forth, beginning with the wheels, is equal to the ground for the colored powder.
The archway (toraṇa) is three times the size of the door and is provided with banners and bells.
With bells and banners fluttering in the wind at the outer corners, the arrangement of the others should be made according to the wheel and as is aesthetically pleasing.
Because he is the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of the Perfectly Awakened One, the eloquent one is known as belonging to the Vajra family. (237–238)

Since the maṇḍala of his mind is utterly pure within the nature of the Dharmakāya, and having taken into account the dispositions of sentient beings, the rules regarding pride and so forth were established;
for since accomplishment arises from wisdom and skillful means, what is the use of restrictions concerning caste and the like? (239)
Starting from one cubit up to a thousand cubits,
having thus laid out the lines for that wheel, one should energize and consecrate the powders with a blazing gaze and the true radiance of previously acquired knowledge.
Oṃ vajracitra samaya hūṃ.
This pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is the liberator of the realm of sentient beings;
it is King Mañjurava himself, the abode of all Tathāgatas.
Completely free from all defects, he is situated within the wheel.
Taking his stand in the northeastern direction, the Guru, with his left fist,
should draw a line— white, yellow, red, green, and black— that is even, clockwise, unbroken, and straight. (242–243)
One should lay down a straight line divided into twenty parts for the door;
if it falls thick, there will be disease; by one that is thin, there is loss of wealth;
by one that is crooked, there is enmity; and by one that is broken, death occurs for both teacher and disciple.
If the falling of the dust is not clockwise, there will be the pinning down by the *rajas* (dust).
A needle made of white vajra, another supported by gold, a needle made of ruby, and likewise another made of emerald [are used]. 245–246.
This sequence of colors within it should be known as follows:
in the east it is great white; in the south, it is joined with yellow;
the western part is red; and in the north, it is joined with madder-red.
In the center, one who is well-composed should always draw the ground-shade, radiant with the luster of sapphire; it consists of wisdom and means,
and the lines should be drawn intersecting one another at intervals of the size of a barley grain.

Crushing all the wicked with the *kuṇḍalāmṛtavajra*, his great mudrā is called the fang; he is the king of mantras, the enemy of the wicked. Homage to the Vajras of the body, speech, and mind of all! Homage to the Vajra Wrathful One, the fierce and terrifying one with great fangs, who holds a sword, a club, an axe, and a noose in his hands! 250.
Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍali! Kha kha! Khāhi khāhi! Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha! Bandha bandha! Hana hana! Daha daha! Garja garja! Visphoṭaya visphoṭaya!
To the one who brings an end to the life of all obstructors and Vināyakas, and of Mahāgaṇapati: Hūṃ Phaṭ!

Having thus drawn the mandala with a seat formed by the moon and sun, one should draw a dark blue sword in the center, radiant with the purity of the [five] primordial wisdoms. To the east, one should draw an eight-spoked wheel, brilliantly shining like a mirror and the other [jewels].
On the right is a jewel, greenish-yellow in color, consisting of nine parts and perfectly even and elevated;
in the west is an eight-petalled lotus, red, representing the [wisdom of] discernment;
and in the north is a fine sword, adorned with the [wisdom of] accomplishment.
By means of skillful methods, the eye [is placed] in the southeast; by virtue of purpose, the vajra in the southwest;
the hideous-faced one in the northwest by force; and the lotus with its stalk in the northeast through wisdom—a yellow [lotus] beautiful with a blue luster.

In the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), on both sides of the eastern gate, [one should place] a mirror, a lute, a vessel for perfumes, a conch, a bed, a garment, and the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), which has been purified by the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth. // 255–256 //
Having thoroughly understood and clearly visualized the mallet of faith and so forth, the staff, the lotus, and the vajra as the fourth, at the gates, one should—
just as before— place the Buddhas within oneself through union with the limbs of wisdom.
Having pervaded the sky with one's own mind and established a seat at the side of the wheel,
one should drive away those obstacles that have arrived by means of them, and having protected [the site],
one should draw [the obstructors] in with Yamāryā and the others, cause them to enter, bind them, and bring them under control. (258–259)
Having presided over the eyes, body, and so forth, and having performed the offering of water (argha), consecration, and worship;
then, having praised, gratified, recited the mantra, and meditated, one should satisfy [the deity].
As before, having prepared the nectar of gnosis within a vessel of a true lotus...
Having worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) established in their respective yogas, one should enter the mandala.
Having become a conqueror of the three worlds (trailokyavijaya), adorned with ornaments and garments as they may be obtained,
and having performed circumambulation and bowed to the wheel (cakra), one should complete [the rite] with the fire-oblation (homa).

Leaving a space of four finger-breadths, the altar—measuring half a cubit or less than a cubit in height—is shaped like a wheel and is suitable for all ritual activities; it is adorned with a blossoming lotus of that same measurement.
The sword [of the altar] is eight or nine finger-breadths in length and height.

In the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the yogin— standing facing the east and surrounded by a circle of vajras— should draw a wheel, a jewel, a lotus, and a sword arranged one within the other. Having recited the mantra of Sarvakṛt and performed the protection, he should place the water for guest-offering (*argha*) and other items on his left, and the remaining items elsewhere.

Having set out the ritual implements and sprinkled them with water, one who possesses the yoga of Mañjuvajra’s nature should kindle a fire fueled by wood from milk-producing trees, purified by the emission of the three syllables.
Having set it ablaze, one should offer *kuśa* grass in a clockwise direction while striking it with the *vyañjana* syllables.
Having meditated upon the Fire-god (Agni) here— born from the seed-syllable *rūṃ*, seated upon a yellow three-cornered lotus in the heart of the first [deity],
yellow in color, with three faces, corpulent, embracing the body of Prajñā, and holding a water-pot,
the gesture of granting fearlessness, a staff, and a rosary in his hands. // 267–268 //
Having invoked the fire of true gnosis as before with the *tritattva-ṭakkin* mantra,
one should perform its sprinkling and other rites, and seat it upon its throne.
Below the handles of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are the *vajra* and *ratna*, and above them [are the other implements].
The *pātrī* vessel is four finger-breadths square, with a vajra-shaped cavity dug two finger-breadths deep.

Inside, at a distance of four finger-breadths from the edge, it has the shape of a lotus petal; within that, there is a cavity one finger-breadth wide for the vajra, and the *sruva* ladle has a lotus petal two finger-breadths wide.
Having meditated upon one's own deity as a blazing seed-syllable within the mouths of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* to it, having placed the letter *ra* at its mouth. One should offer auspicious fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds into the kindled fire.

Then, having first performed the external worship and other rites, one should offer into the fire of the true gnosis of suchness— consisting of pieces of *dūrvā* grass, curd-rice, and *kuśa* grass according to the prescribed sequence— the Lord born from the syllable *maṃ* within the moon of the heart, together with the authentic wheel, while meditating upon him. (273–274)
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni! Of the clarified butter!
Oṃ, to the vajra that burns all sins, burn all sin, svāhā! [This is for] sesame seeds.
Oṃ vajrāyuṣe svāhā. [This is] for the dūrvā grass.
Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrapuṣṭi!
Of unbroken rice grains.
Oṃ, for all prosperity, svāhā!
Of the curd-rice.
Oṃ, to the unimpeded vajra, svāhā! [This is] for the kuśa grasses.
In nourishment, pacification, subjugation, attraction, hatred, expulsion, and malevolent rites;
"Oṃ svāhā hoḥ jaḥ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—at the end of this mantra, there is also the exhortation:
"All the deities are pleased by the Heart-Sattva, their own Lord.
Meditating thus, one should satisfy them with the moon and other substances as before. (275–276)
Having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the tongue [of fire] upon the moon-wheel in the heart, and likewise having sprinkled [the deity],
given water for rinsing the mouth and the *argha* offering, worshipped, and praised, one should dismiss [the deity]. Then,
having offered the remaining sacrificial food (*havya*) into the fire, one whose self is united with yoga should likewise [dismiss] that [fire].
Having dismissed [the deities] according to the previous procedure and having worshipped the maṇḍala, he should enter.
Having first entered himself by means of the ritual for the entry of disciples,
and having performed everything up to the consecration (seka), he should obtain permission from the Lord of the Kula.
The reality arising from great passion and the maṇḍala are like reflections;
for the purpose of admitting the disciple into the city, one should proclaim the reality and the truth.
Because it is the sign of the birth of space, the supreme [reality] is without beginning or end.
O Being consisting of the great vajra, O Mañjuvajra, may you be accomplished for me today!
(281) O supreme among all, O great accomplishment, O presiding deity of great sovereignty! O King who holds all vajras, may the supreme syllable be accomplished for me! (282)

You are faultless and eternal, O Lord who inspires passion for all passions; in reality, you are established for me as Mahārāga, the Great Passion, and Mahārata, the Great Joy. You are the Tathāgata, utterly pure, the pinnacle of all, and liberated from the very beginning.

Samantabhadra, the universal self, you are renowned to me as a Bodhisattva. Through the supreme Great Accomplishment and the mudrā of the pinnacle of great sovereignty, O Vajra, perfected by your great excellence, may the Lord of Vajra-pride be accomplished for me! 284–285
Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, abiding in the hearts of all sentient beings,

and being the father of all sentient beings— he is Kāma, the foremost of those who hold the supreme samaya. By that truth, may there be true gnosis, the maṇḍala whose nature is wisdom and skillful means.
By that truth, O Protector, may you fulfill my desires. (287) All phenomena are like reflections—transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from causes and karma. (288)
"By the truth that [you] have emerged from the reality of suchness, may all the disciples, free from stain, clearly behold the reflection within the mandala.
(289) [The master should visualize] the disciple, who has received the general vows, as previously described, radiant in body and so forth.
The interval between births is said to be [cleansed] by the water from the "all-doing" (sarvakṛt) jar.
Then, O dear one, his face should be covered with red cloth, and he should be asked, "Who are you?
To which the disciple should then reply, O dear one, "I am Subhaga."
Having worshipped the one who offers garlands at the gate and likewise given him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
one should generate the mind of yoga and place the vajra upon the heart with the heart-mantra. (292) [Mantra:]
Oṃ! I generate the mind of all yoga; O Surata, you are the pledge (samaya), Hoḥ! Be accomplished, O Vajra, as you please!
Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
You must not speak of this supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas to one who has not entered the maṇḍala, nor should it be spoken to one who lacks faith—thus it should be said.
Having summoned and caused [the disciple] to enter by means of the respective mantras of Yamāntaka and the others,
one should likewise speak as follows during the reception of the true vows with the five syllables:
"Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas."
Therefore, I shall generate for you the vajra-knowledge by which you will attain even the accomplishments of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments.
You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your samaya be violated. Having thus placed the vajra upon his heart:

This water of yours is hellish; it shall burn you for transgressing the pledge.
Through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment; drink this vajra-amṛta water!
Oṃ vajrodaka ṭhaḥ.
One should speak these words to one who is firm in their vow:

"From this day forward, I am your Vajrapāṇi; whatever I tell you to do must be performed by you, and I am not to be disregarded. Lest, by failing to avoid danger, you should meet your end and fall into hell. Then he should say, "Speak," and [the teacher] should speak to the disciples.
May all the Tathāgatas empower [me], and may Vajrasattva enter me.
Having caused [the disciple] to recite that, one should meditate on a yellow *laṃ* arising from the letter *hūṃ* at the heart, which has the corners marked with a vajra, in the Āhendra [mandala].
The western [mandala] born from *vaṃ* is white, circular, and marked with a water-jar;
the northwestern [mandala] born from *yaṃ* is mobile, resembling a bow marked with a blue banner.
For those two, in the body and speech respectively, there are *haḥ* and *āḥ*; beneath the feet is *jhaiḥ*, blazing intensely.
In the northwest, having kindled with a triangle arising from the syllable *raṃ*, one should enter the disciple:
"Enter! Paralyze! *ra ra ra ra*! Move! *2*! *hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ*!"
Having visualized a red syllable *ĀḤ* on the tongue as possessed [by the deity], one should speak again:
"O Rāgavajra, embracing him, tell me, O Vajra, what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. While making that possession firm, one should say to him: "Stay, O Vajra! (299)
One should cast the garland into the wheel:
"Accept it, O Vajra! Hoḥ!"
One should bind it upon the head:
"O you of great power, accept this being! (300)
Whether at the mark or near the mark, for those who have accepted the garland and those who have not,
one should effect that union through inclination or through their spiritual fitness;
having meditated on the flaming *praṇava* in the eyes.
Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself is now intent upon opening your eyes;
he opens all your eyes with the unsurpassed vajra-eye. (302) Having meditated thus, one should display the wheel.
Beginning with the Lord of the Mandala and continuing as far as Amṛtakuṇḍalin,
one should sprinkle [the disciple] on the head with water while uttering the words "Vajrābhiṣeka.
One should sprinkle him with the crown as before, having first offered the presiding deity.
Having grasped that vajra in the heart, one should also consecrate [the disciple] with the vajra:
"Today you are consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration.
Take this, which is the state of all Buddhas, as the vajra for the sake of perfect accomplishment. (304–305)
Embracing with the vajra and bell by means of one's own lord:
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Vajra Lord; remain, O Vajra, you are the samaya."
On the crown of the head by name.
Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you with the vajra-name empowerment.
He is Amukavajra.
Whatever shines as one's own entire possession, that is Mañjurāj himself;
for phenomena are pure by nature, and he is indeed the accumulation of the Buddha’s gnosis.
Just as the title "Śrī" (Glorious) is applied from the very beginning to the name of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) in his own sovereignty.
But all [deities] ending in Vajra are joined with the syllable *he* due to their universal sovereignty.
Akṣobhya is the purity of the water element; the crown is the essence of equanimity (*samatā*);
the Vajra is the essence of authentic discernment (*pratyavekṣā*); and the Lord is the performer of activities who bestows benefit. // 307–308 //
In this context, knowledge (*jñāna*) is the *vidyā*, the *vajra* is the element (*dhātu*), and the lineage (*gotra*) is indeed the master (*vaśin*).
The vows, the prophecy, and the consolation are included within the *vidyā-secana* (the empowerment of the consort) and the name.
This very state of omniscience resides in the hand of Vajrasattva.
For you too must always maintain the firm vow of Vajrapāṇi. Oṃ! In the vajra-samaya of the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas, remain! I hold you fast: Hīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ!
Having bestowed the vajra-vow upon all, one should cause them to grasp the vajra in its true essence:
"The being without beginning or end is Vajrasattva, the Great Rapture;
he is Samantabhadra, the self of all, the Lord of the Vajra-Arrogance, the Master. (311)
Having grasped the bell according to its true nature, one should know that it is the resonance of wisdom belonging to all Buddhas;
for you too, it must always be maintained, as it is considered by the Victors to be the supreme awakening. 312
One should cause her to play that [instrument] according to its proper method.
(313) For existence is pure by its very nature, yet it is rendered non-existent by [conceptualized] natures; through beings who are truly pure by nature, the supreme existence is brought forth. (314)

Having empowered the Mahāmudrā through the heart-mantras proclaimed for service and so forth, one should recite the mantra without deficiency, by means of the commitments (samaya) such as Kāmarūpa and others,
which possess the nature of self-awareness and are situated in all directions and the three times. (315)
Through union with one's own presiding deity, one should worship both oneself and others.

(316) By means of those difficult observances, when they are practiced, the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) born of the mind, speech, body, and the super-knowledge of invisibility are accomplished. (317)

Therefore, Buddhas and noble beings who practice the supreme conduct of mantra have attained the most excellent syllable of Dharma by means of indulging in all desires. While indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure— which consist of the nature of pleasure, pain, and both— they [attain liberation].
One who seeks knowledge shall indeed accomplish everything through union with those possessed of passion (rāgin).
Whatever other [attainments] are known as inferior arise from the perfection of body, speech, and mind;
they are accomplished through the recitation of mantras and the meditations on body, speech, and mind.
As it has been said:

"Having grasped the vajra according to its true nature and having sounded the bell according to the Dharma, and having empowered the Mahāmudrā according to the Samaya, one should recite the mantra with the heart-mantra. (321)
That has been answered.
To the disciple who has taken the vows but has likewise not yet offered the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā),
one should request the empowerment while bowing with this verse:
"Just as the Great Festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra,"
"O Khavajra and others, grant me [this] also for the sake of my protection!

[Grant it to] the supreme yogin situated upon the lotus of eight petals at the seat of the entrance-gate, together with the wheels of Buddhas born from one's own heart, which pervade all directions and the three times. (323–324)

With those [offerings] accompanied by music, incense, and so forth, as before, one should consecrate the recipient of the Knowledge-consecration with the Great Vajra Consecration, according to this verse:
"The Great Vajra Consecration, honored by the three realms... (325)
I bestow [this] which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.
Having bestowed the irreversible consecration, one should reveal the reality of the wheel;
it is square because of its lack of inequality, due to the equality of the awakened and the unawakened.
Because the phenomena of body, speech, and mind are not joined with [the notions of] multiplicity or unity and so forth,
that mindfulness directed toward them and the faith therein are considered the gateway to awakening. Thereafter,
for the sake of abandoning and the non-arising of errors regarding the past and the future, [one practices].

Furthermore, for the arising and maintenance of the reality that has not yet arisen, there is the gate of the four *vīryas*: zeal (*chanda*), exertion (*utsāha*), stability (*sthiti*), and discernment (*mati*). The last [of these] are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); however, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the gate therein. (329–330)
The incomparable faculties and powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
as well as supreme samādhi, constitute the four gates through these faculties of mindfulness.
Through the four dhyānas, beginning with the first, it becomes like four archways.
The *Śūraṅgama*, *Khagañja*, and other such samādhis are considered the railings (*vedikā*).
On the altar (*vedi*) is the assembly of those who hold books and so forth, intent on performing worship;
because of those various ornaments, all aspirations are fulfilled. (332–333)
It resounds with the voice of the ninefold True Dharma shaken forth by the Vinaya;
it is made to ring by the bells upon the crest-banners of the universe shaken by the wind.
Through the mirror-like wisdom and the factors of enlightenment, it shines radiantly in all directions.
Resplendent with necklaces, half-necklaces, the moon, the sun, mirrors, garlands, and chowries; within that [palace],
there is a wheel resembling eight mandalas, supported by the excellent pillars of the seven jewels, beginning with the wheel-jewel, which have been purified by the eight liberations.
Because it sets in motion the Vajrayāna of the perfectly awakened ones of all directions, times, and realms,
it is encircled on all sides by a vajra-line and is perfectly circular.
The five colors are the five Buddhas, because through their gnoses they delight sentient beings.

Through the complete purification of the sense faculties, their objects, and so forth, and by means of the discernment of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), that which was previously drunk as the nectar of gnosis by the Vajra-holders became a full vase; it is the outflow of the fulfillment of the accumulations, made moist with compassion. // 338–339 //
That which is called flowers, incense, great lamps, and perfumes in the maṇḍala is the mass of fame consisting of the torches of Dharma that gladden with the blossoms of the factors of enlightenment;
the food offering is the nourishment of Dharma, while modesty and shame constitute the restraint.
It increases great bliss through beautiful song, dance, and instrumental music.
Because it is the city of liberation, it is the "City" (pura); because it gathers the essence, it is the "Maṇḍala.
Having demonstrated the reality of the wheel, one should point out the reality of the deity. // 341–342 //
Through the purity of faith, vigor, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and [wisdom], he possesses the form of the six waters;
through the purity of wisdom, the mind of the one who maintains yoga in the body and so forth is perfectly stainless.
Through the external purity of the six [perfections] beginning with generosity, he maintains the state of Rūpavajra and the others.
Because it is the cause for the protection of the world and so forth, it has the nature of the eye and the other [senses].

Through the purity of the cognition that arises from the conceptualization of objects, sentient beings, self, and [mental] constructs, there is the Mirror-like Wisdom and the others, which constitute the essential nature of all Buddhas. (344–345)
Through the yoga of the non-arising of cognition, it is radiant in the form of the Lord of the Wheel;
through the complete purification of the delusions regarding form and so forth, it consists of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements;
and through the transformation of stinginess and other afflictions, it is firmly established within the supreme elements.
Through the transformation of its own opposites, it is stainless and complete with the powers and so forth.
Because it is non-conceptual, it possesses profundity; because it brings about the welfare of both self and others, it possesses magnificence.
Due to this profundity and magnificence, this mind is considered to consist of wisdom and skillful means.
Because it is a reality to be personally realized within oneself, it does not abide in distinctions such as difference or non-difference.
When things are thus elaborated, the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth are merely the fruits of delusion.
Therefore, through the union with the foremost of commitments, which is endowed with the qualities of the ocean of forms, [one attains the goal].
Having performed this, the master should lie down there and effect the penetration of gnosis (jñānāveśa).
Having struck the lotus with the vajra and caused the Buddhas to enter within himself,

Uttering his own name, the Vajra-Self should cause [the deities] to radiate forth through the yoga of the wheel;
