Having praised [the deities] with the gatekeepers and performed the rite of the gateway, one should accomplish [the practice] here.
Having performed the empowerment of the eyes, body, and so forth, as well as the consecrations and worship, one should request:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, act for the attainment of all siddhis! (353–354)
Having properly drawn the wheel, this is the procedure for the initial consecration;

however, for images, books, and so forth, it extends up to the *pauruṣa* rite following the sprinkling (*seka*). Furthermore, that which is prescribed—such as the complete offering of *argha*, the canopy, the protection rites, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and so on—[is to be performed].
Having performed the external bath with the three, five, or six-syllable mantras previously extracted,
just as a universal monarch [performs his own],
this indeed is the supreme reality which consists of wisdom and means.

The *niṣyanda* [empowerment] is the water-crown; the *pāka* [empowerment] consists of the Vajra-lords; the *pauruṣa* empowerment is conferred by the Perfect Buddhas; and the *vaimalya* [empowerment] arises from the secret yoga.
Then, [one should take] a woman endowed with beauty and other qualities, who is well-practiced in the yoga of the maṇḍala circle.
Having empowered that [consort] who abides in the samaya-restraint as the mudrā of the wheel,

and having caused the host of lords of sages to enter within the vajra with sublime bliss, one should press [the consort] with the ring and little fingers and cause [the substance] to fall into the mouth of the disciple.
The disciple of firm intellect should drink everything with the nature of Vairocana;
he becomes the universal one like the universe itself, exclaiming here, "Oh, what bliss!
Through contact with wisdom, the glorious one should perceive the reality.
This delightful dhāraṇī of yours was devised by the Buddhas for practice;
through the application of the sequence of the wheel, experience the sublime bliss while gazing at the mind within the jewel from the vajraparyaṅka posture.
Having explained the mandala, the reality of the deities, and the preparatory rites for the preceptor,
and having consecrated [the disciple] with the secret and wisdom [empowerments], one should point out the reality.
As it is said:
Neither through the practices for awakening and so forth, nor through any other auspicious deeds,
are all the Buddhas and others attained as they are through this method of empowerment.
One should guard the pledge of the Master and always maintain the vow of restraint.

The nectar of the five meats is to be consumed; furthermore, there is a samaya for the Rākṣasa. The destruction of jewels, the killing [of enemies], the taking of all women, the seizing of others' property, and false speech—this indeed must be observed according to the rules, as it is prescribed in the Yoga-tantra.
Then, having become a Tathāgata, one should perform the prophecy with this [mantra]:
With the left hand forming the heart-fist and holding the robe, and the right hand granting the boon— Oṃ! I, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, prophesy you thus.
Having extracted [beings] from the miserable states of existence, for the sake of attaining ultimate liberation from cyclic existence:
O Vajra-named Tathāgata, for the sake of accomplishment, *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.
By means of this, the mantra-master who is the lord of the entire world is prophesied;
indeed, he shall be prophesied by the Sugatas for supreme enlightenment.
For in whatever way sentient beings proceed toward discipline according to their own nature, [so shall he be].
For in that very way, one who is pure through passion and the other [afflictions] should act for the sake of sentient beings.
371 Practicing the yoga of the three samādhis four times every day at the junctions of the day, having become so, accomplish the common and other attainments. 372

One possessing the power of invisibility [acts] within a thousandfold world-system; one possessing the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), within two thousandfold world-systems; a *vidyādhara*, within three thousandfold world-systems; and the Vajra-holder, the Lord of all the world.
Whatever rite is desired—be it pacification, enrichment, or any other—[is accomplished].
By means of the yoga of passion for the wheel, one who practices succeeds quickly.
Thus it has been said: [374]
All the Vajra Lords, who contemplate the reality of the essence of passion,
bring about the awakening born of passion for the sake of seeking the welfare of all sentient beings.
Therefore, the practitioner of mantra who seeks awakening [should apply] the activities of body, speech, and mind.
One should perform all ritual actions according to the prescribed rule; all that is intended for the sake of awakening.
Just as [it was taught] to the disciples who have entered [the path] and who desire the benefits, one should likewise bestow the threefold pledge of consolation according to the rule. (376–377)
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today liberated from all sins and well-established.
There shall be no further death for you from this Great Bliss vehicle.
"Invincible and unbound, rejoice, free from fear on every side!
Your suffering in existence has ceased for the sake of ultimate purification from existence;
you have become the foremost among teachers for the sake of the final accomplishment of liberation from existence."
This perfected commitment of the samaya must be constantly guarded by you.
This supreme and eternal command has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas together:
"The *bodhicitta* must never be abandoned, as it is the seal (*mudrā*) known as the Vajra. (381)
By the mere production of which one becomes a Buddha indeed, there is no doubt.
The true Dharma is never to be rejected nor ever to be abandoned;
yet, out of ignorance or delusion, one must certainly not fail to reveal it. (382–383)

One should not abandon one's own self nor afflict it with ascetic penances; one should maintain happiness according to one's ease, for this is the future Fully Awakened One. The vajra, the bell, and the mudrā must never be abandoned.
The teacher is not to be despised, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
Whoever would despise the teacher, the guru who is equal to all the Buddhas,
shall always encounter suffering by having insulted all the Buddhas.
By fevers, poisons, toxins, diseases, the afflictions of *ḍākinīs*,
planetary influences, obstacles, and terrible *vināyakas*, one who has been slain shall go to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, [one should honor] the Vajrācārya, the great guru.
One should never despise a person whose excellence is concealed.
You should give what is appropriate, accompanied by devotion to the guru and a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā);
for then fevers and other afflictions will no longer prevail.
One's own commitment must always be accomplished; likewise, the Tathāgatas must always be worshipped;
and one must always give to the guru, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
From that giving comes the accumulation of merit, and from that accumulation comes supreme enlightenment.
By giving this, it becomes a perpetual gift given to all the Buddhas.
Today your birth has become fruitful, since you are well-established in this;
you will undoubtedly become equal to the deities of the Samaya. // 391-392 //
Today the Venerable Ones have been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Holders of the Vajra;
they are firm sovereigns, lords of kingship over the great realm of the three worlds.
Today, having utterly conquered the Māras, they have entered the supreme city.
"Buddhahood has been attained by you this very day; there is no doubt in this.
Thus, make your minds into the diamond of serene faith and partake in your own samaya, which bestows inexhaustible bliss.
Having now reached a state equal to Vajrasattva—eternal and swift in bringing happiness to the world—you have become so."
Having prostrated at the feet of the guru, the disciples, who are devoted and affectionate toward the virtuous, should say: "O Lord, we shall do exactly as you command.
This should be done by each of them individually with their left hand, provided that it is possible.
Holding the right thumb [of the disciple], one should perform the rite of pacification according to the prescribed rule.
Having offered either twenty-one oblations or a single oblation for the king or the sovereign,
and having likewise offered for the pacification of the guardians of the directions and of oneself, one should request the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having gathered assistance for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all beings, or for each [task] such as learning and so forth,
or for earth, elephants, gold, and the like, or for one's own success—
having satisfied them by giving sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā)— whatever was relinquished [for that purpose], [that is the merit]. // 399 //
One should worship the wheel with all those foods and activities, both one's own and those of others.
Having gathered worthy and excellent disciples, and having satisfied them with various supreme offerings, one should withdraw [the visualization] with the three syllables ending in the letter *muḥ*.

Having given that supreme wheel, which is empty by means of the mantra beginning with "ākāra," to one who requests it, one should cast a small amount of powder into water; [then] one should create a great amount of powder.
Whatever wealth is used for filling the pit, for the consecration, for the fire offering, and for the wheel—
"The Master alone possesses all of that," said the Holder of the Supreme Vajra (Varavajradhṛk).
This clear procedure for the wheel has been taught for the beginner;
however, for one who has well-attained the descent of gnosis, it is explained by means of that very descent itself. 403–404.
Having initiated and fully worshipped a boy and a girl at the age of twelve,
one should consider the wheel that they perform through mind, speech, and body.
Regarding the mind, the instruction for Akṣobhya and Māmakī is proclaimed.
In the speech of Pāṇḍarā and Amitā, and in the body of Śāśvata and Locanā—this [practice] is marvelous because of the arrangement of the compression of mind, speech, and body.
From the compression of the mind comes thorough knowledge; from the compression of speech comes the recitation of mantras.
From the paralysis of the body comes the state of being struck with wonder; this is the procedure for the entry of that paralysis.
Herein, the consecration of the master and the disciple is established according to the previously mentioned method.
One who has attained mastery over knowledge should, by means of the mind alone, bring the three wheels under control.
Since the wheel is perceived by both oneself and others through its empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna),
entry into it is permitted and is held to be like a vivid dream.
Therefore, it should be known as supreme because of the firmness of the mental form.
The procedure for the wheels of speech and body is also as before for those of the three yogas;
in their place, the symbol of Akṣobhya should appear for the purification of the secrets of speech and body.
This applies even to those who have attained mastery over the wisdom, action, and union [mudrās].
The entire ritual procedure is performed by the mind alone; without that, it is not accomplished at all.

For the foremost disciples of the Vajrācārya, whose nature is devoted to the [four] results beginning with the natural outflow (niṣyanda), the mental procedure is supreme; what could be achieved here by mere words? (412–413)
Buddhahood does not arise from mere conduct, nor does it come from mere learning;
it is not attained even through reflection, but is said to result from meditative cultivation.
As it has been said: [413]
Enough with this overly prolix discourse for the practitioners of mantra;
the mind is what must be mastered, for from the mind alone arises perfect awakening.
As it has been said: [414]
That fruit which is the bodhicitta is the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha;
it consists of Vajrasattva, manifested as the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body.
Apart from the cessation of ordinary conceptualization, there is no other suffering inherent in cyclic existence.
Thus, its direct opponent consists of wisdom and means. [... 416
